notes.short: The rich man fades “like a flower of the field”
notes.about: James tells the rich man to exult in his low position, for he will pass away like a flower of the field. The scorching sun withers the plant and its beauty is lost. So riches and worldly splendor pass quickly and give no ground for pride. Isaiah 40:6-8 uses the same picture.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: he will pass away like a flower of the field
figure.means: riches and worldly splendor, which pass away as quickly as a wild flower withers in the heat

notes.evidence: Barnes says the comparison of worldly splendor with the fading flower of the field is common in Scripture, and that James probably had Isaiah 40:6-8 in mind. Calvin says the meaning is that glorying in riches is foolish, since they pass away in a moment. Clarke calls the picture a metaphor whose sense is plain: all human things pass away, and earthly possessions with them.
notes.limit: The writers differ on Isaiah 40:6-8: one thinks James probably had it in mind; another allows an allusion but not a quotation, since Isaiah speaks of the whole man and James of the pomp of riches.

cites.quote: Because as the flower of the grass he shall pass away - That is, since it is a fact that he will thus pass away, he should rejoice that he is reminded of it. ... The comparison of worldly splendor with the fading flower of the field, is one that is common in Scripture. It is probable that James had his eye on the passage in Isa 40:6-8
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: As the flower of the grass. Were any one to say that James alludes to the words of Isaiah, I would not much object; but I cannot allow that he quotes the testimony of the Prophet ... but here what is spoken of is the pomp of wealth or of riches. And the meaning is, that glorying in riches is foolish and preposterous, because they pass away in a moment.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: For the sun is no sooner risen - We need not pursue this metaphor, as St. James' meaning is sufficiently clear: All human things are transitory; rise and fall, or increase and decay, belong to all the productions of the earth, and to all its inhabitants. ... Earthly possessions are subject to similar mutations.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Desire conceives and gives birth to sin
notes.about: Desire is pictured as a woman who conceives and gives birth to sin; and sin, once full-grown, gives birth to death. The picture shows that sin starts in a person's own desire, not from God (verse 13), and grows until it ends in death.

figure.name: Personification
figure.words: after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death
figure.means: sin starts when a person's own desire is given its way, and it grows until it ends in death

original.note: In James's Greek the verbs are those of childbearing: one for conceiving and two for giving birth, the second used of sin bringing forth death.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Personification, human actions given to things. Albert Barnes says the allusion is obvious: when desire is acted on, sin is produced, so sin is not to be traced to God. Adam Clarke says the Greek verbs show the figure of conceiving and bringing forth. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) pictures desire as a harlot who brings forth sin.
notes.limit: Not all the writers name the figure, and one calls it a metaphor; they agree on what it shows.

cites.at: Prosopopoeia: human actions given to things, p. 869
cites.quote: “When lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin.” See under Climax.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The allusion here is obvious. The meaning is, when the desire which we have naturally is quickened, or made to act, the result is that sin is produced. … The design of all this is to show that sin is not to be traced to God, but to man himself … The result of sin when it is fully carried out, is death
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: When the evil propensity works unchecked, it bringeth forth sin - the evil act between the parties is perpetrated. … Any person acquainted with the import of the verbs συλλαμβανειν, τικτειν , and αποκυειν, will see that this is the metaphor, and that I have not exhausted it.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The guilty union is committed by the will embracing the temptress. "Lust," the harlot, then, "brings forth sin," namely, of that kind to which the temptation inclines.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Like a man who forgets his face in a mirror
notes.about: One who hears the word but does not do it is like a man who looks at his face in a mirror, goes away, and at once forgets what he looks like. God's word shows us what we are, but a passing glance soon fades. The one who looks intently into the perfect law and keeps doing it will be blessed.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: is like a man who looks at his face in a mirror
figure.means: the hearer who sees himself in God's word for a moment but, not doing it, soon forgets what it showed him

notes.evidence: Calvin calls it a striking comparison: teaching only heard, not taken into the heart, soon vanishes. Barnes says the ground of the comparison is plain: the word of God is like a mirror held up before us. Clarke calls it a simple, expressive metaphor, God's doctrines being such a mirror. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the hearer sees his moral face in God's Word as in a mirror.

cites.quote: Heavenly doctrine is indeed a mirror in which God presents himself to our view ... But here he speaks of the external glance of the eye, not of the vivid and efficacious meditation which penetrates into the heart. It is a striking comparison, by which he briefly intimates, that a doctrine merely heard and not received inwardly into the heart avails nothing, because it soon vanishes away.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: For if any be ... - The ground of the comparison in these verses is obvious. The apostle refers to what all persons experience, the fact that we do not retain a distinct impression of ourselves after we have looked in a mirror. ... So when we hear the word of God. It is like a mirror held up before us. ... But we turn away immediately, and forget it all.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Beholding his natural face in a glass - This metaphor is very simple, but very expressive. ... The doctrines of God, faithfully preached, are such a mirror; he who hears cannot help discovering his own character, and being affected with his own deformity; he sorrows, and purposes amendment; but when the preaching is over, the mirror is removed
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: As a man may behold his natural face in a mirror, so the hearer may perceive his moral visage in God's Word. This faithful portraiture of man's soul in Scripture, is the strongest proof of the truth of the latter.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Kind words that leave the hungry unfed
notes.about: James pictures a brother or sister without clothes or food who is sent off with kind words and given nothing. Such words do them no good. In the same way, he says, faith that does nothing is dead (2:17): a claim to faith without deeds is as empty as wishing the hungry well.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: Go in peace; stay warm and well fed
figure.means: a faith that only speaks: as useless as kind words to the needy that give them nothing

notes.evidence: Calvin says James compares this shadowy faith to bidding a famished man be filled with no food. Barnes calls the comparison obvious and striking: faith without deeds is just as useless. Clarke says the words help the needy as much as faith without works helps at the judgment. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says kind words without deeds profit no one, nor does faith of mere profession.

cites.quote: he compares this shadowy faith to the saying of one who bids a famished man to be filled without supplying him with the food of which he is destitute. As, then, he who sends away a poor man with words, and offers him no help, treats him with mockery, so they who devise for themselves faith without works, and without any of the duties of religion, trifle with God.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The comparison in these verses is very obvious and striking. The sense is, that faith in itself, without the acts that correspond to it, and to which it would prompt, is as cold, and heartless, and unmeaning, and useless, as it would be to say to one who was destitute of the necessaries of life ... In the case of one who was hungry or naked, what he wanted was not good wishes or kind words merely
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Be ye warmed and filled - Your saying so to them, while you give them nothing, will just profit them as much as your professed faith, without those works which are the genuine fruits of true faith, will profit you in the day when God comes to sit in judgment upon your soul.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Just retribution: kind professions unaccompanied with corresponding acts, as they are of no "profit" to the needy object of them, so are of no profit to the professor himself. So faith consisting in mere profession is unacceptable to God, the object of faith, and profitless to the possessor.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: A small bit guides a whole horse
notes.about: James points to the bit in a horse's mouth: a small thing, yet with it we guide the whole animal. In the same way the tongue is a small part of the body (3:5), yet it has great power over the whole life, and the one who rules his tongue can rule himself (3:2).

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: we put bits into the mouths of horses
figure.means: the tongue: a small member, yet the one who bridles it can guide his whole self

notes.evidence: Calvin says James likens the tongue to a bridle, then to a helm: as a bridled horse turns at its rider's will, so the tongue can govern a man. Barnes calls it a simple illustration: as a small bit controls a horse, so the tongue the body. Clarke says the tongue must be bridled as the horse is. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says man turns his whole body with the little tongue.

cites.quote: By these two comparisons he proves that a great part of true perfection is in the tongue, and that it exercises dominion, as he has just said, over the whole life. He compares the tongue, first, to a bridle, and then to a helm of a ship. Though a horse be a ferocious animal, yet he is turned about at the will of its rider, because he is bridled; no less can the tongue serve to govern man.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The meaning of this simple illustration is, that as we control a horse by the bit - though the bit is a small thing - so the body is controlled by the tongue. He who has a proper control over his tongue can govern his whole body, as he who holds a bridle governs and turns about the horse.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: he proceeds to show that the tongue must be bridled as the horse, and governed as the ships; because, though it is small, it is capable of ruling the whole man; and of irritating and offending others.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: we put the bits (so literally, "the customary bits") into their mouths that they may obey us, we turn about also their whole body. This is to illustrate how man turns about his whole body with the little tongue.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: A very small rudder steers a great ship
notes.about: Ships are large and driven by strong winds, yet a very small rudder steers them wherever the pilot wants. So the tongue, a small part of the body (3:5), has great power over the whole person. The strong winds can picture the passions that drive a man, which a ruled tongue holds in check.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: they are steered by a very small rudder
figure.means: the tongue: a small member that, rightly ruled, guides the whole person, as the helm turns a great ship against the winds

notes.evidence: Calvin says James likens the tongue to a ship's helm, which guides a large vessel against the winds: the small tongue does much to rule life. Barnes calls it a striking illustration of the tongue, and reads the winds as the passions. Clarke says the tongue must be governed as ships are. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the feeling moving the tongue answers to the steersman's will.
notes.limit: Only one of these writers reads the strong winds as the passions; the others do not say what the winds stand for.

cites.quote: By these two comparisons he proves that a great part of true perfection is in the tongue ... He compares the tongue, first, to a bridle, and then to a helm of a ship. ... So also with regard to the helm of a ship, which guides a large vessel and surmounts the impetuosity of winds. Though the tongue be a small member, yet it avails much in regulating the life of man.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Behold also the ships - This illustration is equally striking and obvious. ... So with the tongue. ... It is probable that by the "fierce winds" here as impelling the ship, the apostle meant to illustrate the power of the passions in impelling man. Even a man under impetuous passion would be restrained, if the tongue is properly controlled, as the ship driven by the winds is by the helm.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: he proceeds to show that the tongue must be bridled as the horse, and governed as the ships; because, though it is small, it is capable of ruling the whole man; and of irritating and offending others.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Not only animals, but even ships. the governor listeth--literally, "the impulse of the steersman pleaseth." The feeling which moves the tongue corresponds with this.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The tongue is like a small fire in a great forest
notes.about: James likens the tongue to a small spark that sets a great forest ablaze. It is a small part of the body, yet its words can spread harm far and wide. Verse 6 carries the picture on: the tongue is a fire that pollutes the whole person and sets the course of life on fire.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: how small a spark sets a great forest ablaze
figure.means: the tongue: a small member whose words can kindle harm far and wide, as a little fire kindles a great pile

original.note: In James's Greek the word rendered forest, hulē, means a wood or forest, and also firewood or fuel; two of the writers take it here as a great heap of wood or fuel.

notes.evidence: John Calvin says the tongue, if wanton and violent, destroys all things like a fire, and that James calls it a little fire to show its harm reaches far. Albert Barnes says a very little fire kindles a large pile, and the tongue has effects like that. Joseph Benson says James shows the work of the tongue by another comparison, a little fire kindling a great flame.

cites.quote: if it be petulant and violent, like a fire it destroys all things. He represents it as a small or little fire, to intimate that this smallness of the tongue will not be a hindrance that its power should not extend far and wide to do harm.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The Greek word ὕλην hulēn, means a wood, forest, grove; and then fire-wood, fuel. This is the meaning here. The sense is, that a very little fire is sufficient to ignite a large quantity of combustible materials, and that the tongue produces effects similar to that. A spark will kindle a lofty pile; and a word spoken by the tongue may set a neighborhood or a village "in a flame."
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: So the tongue is a little , and apparently insignificant member, and yet boasteth great things Hath great influence: also, to show by another comparison the operation of the tongue, behold how great a matter How great a quantity of wood and other materials; a little fire kindleth Into a terrible flame.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: No spring gives both fresh and salt water
notes.about: James asks whether one spring can pour out both fresh and salt water, or a fig tree grow olives. Nature does not mix such things, yet one mouth both blesses God and curses people made in His likeness (verses 9 and 10). The likenesses from nature show how wrong that is.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: Can both fresh water and salt water flow from the same spring?
figure.means: a mouth that both blesses God and curses people, a mixing that nature itself does not allow

notes.evidence: John Calvin says these comparisons show a cursing tongue is monstrous, against all nature. Albert Barnes says a fig tree bears only figs, and so the tongue should utter one kind of feeling. Adam Clarke says nature shows no such inconsistency as blessing and cursing in man. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls the fountain an image of the heart, its opening of the mouth.
notes.limit: The copies differ in the last words of verse 12, and scholars differ on the reading.

cites.quote: He adduces these comparisons in order to shew that a cursing tongue is something monstrous, contrary to all nature, and subverts the order everywhere established by God. For God hath so arranged things which are contrary, that inanimate things ought to deter us from a chaotic mixture, sure as is found in a double tongue.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Such a thing is impossible in nature, and equally absurd in morals. A fig-tree bears only figs; and so the tongue ought to give utterance only to one class of sentiments and emotions. These illustrations are very striking, and show the absurdity of that which the apostle reproves.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: In many things nature is a sure guide to man; but no such inconsistency is found in the natural world as this blessing and cursing in man. No fountain, at the same opening, sends forth sweet water and bitter; no fig tree can bear olive berries; no vine can bear figs ... These are all contradictions, and indeed impossibilities, in nature.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: fountain--an image of the heart: as the aperture (so the Greek for "place" is literally) of the fountain is an image of man's mouth. The image here is appropriate to the scene of the Epistle, Palestine, wherein salt and bitter springs are found.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Patient like a farmer waiting for the rains
notes.about: James sets a farmer before his readers. Once he has sown, he waits through the fall and spring rains for the precious crop, for he cannot hurry the harvest. So believers are to wait patiently, and strengthen their hearts, until the Lord's coming (verse 8).

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: See how the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the soil
figure.means: believers, who must bear wrongs and delay patiently, waiting for the harvest the Lord will bring at His coming

notes.evidence: John Calvin calls the farmer a similitude: as he waits calmly for the harvest, we should wait for the day of the Lord without fretting. Albert Barnes says the farmer cannot hasten his crop, and so we should wait for what is in God's own keeping. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it an image of bearing toil and delay in hope of the harvest at last.

cites.quote: Paul briefly refers to the same similitude ... when he says that the husbandman ought to labor before he gathers the fruit; but James more fully expresses the idea ... He hence concludes, that we ought not to be immoderately anxious, if we must now labor and sow, until the harvest as it were comes, even the day of the Lord.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The farmer waits patiently for the grain to grow. It requires time to mature the crop, and he does not become impatient. ... We cannot control the rain, the sun, the season; and the farmer therefore patiently waits until in the regular course of events he has a harvest. So we cannot control and hasten the events which are in God's own keeping
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: unto the coming of the Lord--Christ, when the trial of your patience shall cease. husbandman waiteth for--that is, patiently bears toils and delays through hope of the harvest at last. Its "preciousness" (compare Psa 126:6, "precious seed") will more than compensate for all the past. Compare the same image, Gal 6:3, Gal 6:9.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)
